definition: bad-tempered and unfriendly

examples.text: The surly ferryman takes their coins without a word of thanks.
Surly crowds watched in silence as the tax collectors rode in.
I am surly before breakfast and should not be asked questions.

confused.note: Surly means bad-tempered; surely means certainly.

questions.passage: Regulars at the diner have learned to ignore the cook's ______ manner. He grunts in place of greeting, slams plates on the counter, and has not been known to smile since the place opened.
questions.explanation: Grunting and slamming plates show a bad-tempered, unfriendly manner.

distractors.why: Gullible means easily fooled, which is not what the details show.
Hallowed means sacred, which does not describe a grumpy cook.
Diminutive means very small, which does not fit.

definition: to suggest that something is true as a starting point for reasoning

examples.text: Physicists postulated the particle's existence decades before it was detected.
The historian postulates that the plague arrived by sea.
I postulate that the missing cookies and my brother's crumbs are related.

confused.note: To postulate is to propose as a basis for reasoning; to populate is to fill with people.

questions.passage: To explain why the outer planets moved as they did, astronomers ______ the existence of an unseen world beyond them. The search this idea inspired led, in 1846, to the discovery of Neptune.
questions.explanation: Proposing an unseen planet as an explanation is suggesting it as a basis for reasoning.

distractors.why: Rectified means corrected, which does not fit proposing an unseen world.
Feigned means pretended, which is not what the astronomers did.
Perpetuated means caused to continue, which does not fit.

definition: to pretend to feel or be something

examples.text: The fox feigns sleep until the hen wanders close.
The general feigned a retreat to draw the enemy out of the fort.
I feigned surprise at the party I had known about for weeks.

confused.note: To feign is to pretend; a feint is a deceptive move in a fight or game.

questions.passage: The opossum has an unusual defense. When cornered by a predator it will ______ death, lying motionless with its mouth open until the attacker loses interest and moves on.
questions.explanation: Lying still to look dead is pretending.

distractors.why: Revere means to respect deeply, which does not fit.
Surmount means to overcome, which is not what the animal does to death.
Abase means to humiliate, which does not fit.

definition: to judge the value, quality, or nature of something

examples.text: A jeweler was called to appraise the crown before it was sold.
The team appraised the damage to the reef after the storm.
The mechanic appraised the old car and suggested we keep walking.

confused.note: To appraise is to judge the value of; to apprise is to inform.

questions.passage: Before the estate could be divided among the heirs, an expert was hired to ______ its contents. She spent a week examining the furniture, paintings, and silver and assigning a price to each piece.
questions.explanation: Examining items and assigning prices is judging their value.

distractors.why: Apprise means to inform; it resembles the right word but does not mean to value.
Feign means to pretend, which does not fit.
Perpetuate means to make something continue, which does not fit.

definition: young and lacking experience of life

examples.text: The callow lieutenant is no match for the old sergeant's cunning.
The council dismissed the heir as a callow youth unfit to rule.
At fourteen I was too callow to realize the "free trial" would bill my mom.

confused.note: Callow means inexperienced; callous means unfeeling.

questions.passage: Looking back, the diplomat admitted that she had been ______ when she took her first post. She had assumed that good intentions were enough and had not yet learned how often they are misread.
questions.explanation: Naive assumptions from early in her career show inexperience.

distractors.why: Callous means unfeeling; it looks like the right word but she was naive, not cruel.
Obtuse means slow to understand; her fault was lack of experience.
Surly means bad-tempered, which is not what she admits.

definition: to deal successfully with a difficulty; to overcome

examples.text: The expedition surmounted hunger, frostbite, and a mutiny to reach the pole.
Engineers surmounted the problem of heat by lining the capsule with ceramic tiles.
I surmounted my fear of public speaking one shaky sentence at a time.

confused.note: To surmount is to overcome; amount is a quantity.

questions.passage: The obstacles facing the young rower were considerable: she had no coach, no sponsor, and a boat borrowed from a neighbor. She ______ them all, winning the national title within three years.
questions.explanation: Winning despite the obstacles means she overcame them.

distractors.why: Perpetuated means made something continue, the opposite of getting past obstacles.
Appraised means judged the value of, which does not fit.
Postulated means proposed as a premise, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin mons, "mountain": to climb over

definition: to lower someone in rank, dignity, or self-respect; to humiliate

examples.text: The conqueror abased the defeated king by making him walk behind the baggage carts.
She refuses to abase herself by begging the landlord for more time.
I will not abase myself by asking my little sister for a ride.

confused.note: To abase is to humiliate; to abate is to lessen.

questions.passage: The proud minister had never apologized to anyone. To keep his post, however, he was forced to ______ himself before the assembly, admitting his errors aloud and asking its members for forgiveness.
questions.explanation: Publicly admitting error and begging forgiveness lowers his dignity.

distractors.why: Exalt means to raise in rank or praise, the opposite of humbling oneself.
Amass means to gather a large amount, which does not fit.
Warrant means to justify, which does not fit "himself before the assembly."

definition: full of energy and new ideas; continuously changing

examples.text: A coral reef is a dynamic system in which every species affects the others.
Under its dynamic young mayor, the city built three bridges in five years.
Our dynamic new coach has us running drills I have never seen before.

confused.note: Dynamic means energetic or changing; dynastic relates to a ruling family.

questions.passage: The exhibition presents the ocean not as a fixed backdrop but as a ______ system. Currents shift with the seasons, temperatures rise and fall, and whole populations of fish move thousands of miles in response.
questions.explanation: Shifting currents and migrating fish show constant change.

distractors.why: Static means unchanging, the "fixed backdrop" the exhibition rejects.
Diminutive means tiny, which the ocean is not.
Sinister means threatening, which is not the contrast with "fixed."

definition: to make an action seem reasonable or necessary; to justify

examples.text: The preliminary results warrant a larger study.
The governor judged that the unrest did not warrant sending troops.
A paper cut does not warrant a trip to the emergency room.

confused.note: To warrant is to justify; a warranty is a written guarantee for a product.

questions.passage: A single cracked tile hardly ______ replacing the entire floor. The contractor suggested swapping out the damaged piece, which would take an hour and cost a fraction as much.
questions.explanation: "Hardly" plus the cheaper fix shows the damage does not justify replacing everything.

distractors.why: Rectifies means corrects, which does not fit a tile and a floor.
Feigns means pretends, which a tile cannot do.
Embellishes means decorates or exaggerates, which does not fit.

definition: the ability to behave or speak carefully so as not to cause embarrassment; or the freedom to decide

examples.text: The envoy was chosen for his discretion; he had never repeated a secret.
The butler's discretion is absolute, and the family's scandals die with him.
Spending the prize money is at your discretion.

confused.note: Discretion is careful judgment; discrete means separate. Discreet, the related adjective, means tactful.

questions.passage: The lawyer was valued above all for her ______. Clients knew that whatever they told her, however embarrassing, would never be repeated outside her office.
questions.explanation: Never repeating clients' secrets shows careful, tactful judgment.

distractors.why: Fortitude means courage in hardship, which is not the quality described.
Levity means lightheartedness, which is not why clients trusted her.
A penchant is a strong liking, which does not fit.

definition: copied from something else and so not original

examples.text: Critics called the novel derivative, a patchwork of better books.
The palace's design was derivative of the French court's.
The new superhero movie felt derivative, right down to the final battle in the sky.

confused.note: Derivative means unoriginal; derisive means mocking.

questions.passage: The band's first album was dismissed as ______. Reviewers pointed out that its melodies, its lyrics, and even its cover photograph closely resembled those of a more famous group.
questions.explanation: An album that closely copies another group's work is unoriginal.

distractors.why: Dynamic means energetic, which is not why reviewers dismissed it.
Unequivocal means clear and firm, which does not describe an imitative album.
Hallowed means sacred, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin rivus, "stream": drawn off from a source

definition: seeming evil or dangerous; threatening harm

examples.text: A sinister figure waits at the end of the alley, hat pulled low.
The quiet closing of the newspapers was the first sinister sign of what was to come.
The basement looks sinister with the lights off, but it is only the furnace.

confused.note: Sinister means threatening; sinuous means winding or curving.

questions.passage: At first the villagers took the stranger's questions for simple curiosity. They began to suspect a more ______ purpose when they noticed that he asked only about which houses stood empty and which families were away.
questions.explanation: Interest in empty houses suggests a threatening purpose.

distractors.why: Callow means inexperienced, which is not what they suspected.
Hallowed means holy, the opposite of a harmful purpose.
Diminutive means tiny, which does not describe a purpose.

definition: a person who thinks and acts independently, not following the group

examples.text: The senator was a maverick who voted against his own party as often as with it.
Once a maverick, she saw her theory become the textbook explanation.
My sister is the family maverick: the only one who refuses to watch football.

confused.note: A maverick is an independent thinker; a renegade has deserted a cause or group.

questions.passage: The architect was a ______ in a profession that prized conformity. While her colleagues designed glass towers, she built low houses of rammed earth and refused every commission that required steel.
questions.explanation: Going her own way against her profession makes her an independent thinker.

distractors.why: A harbinger is a sign of something to come, which is not what the examples show.
A ruse is a trick, not a person.
A penchant is a liking, not a person.

definition: spread out over a large area; or using too many words and not clearly organized

examples.text: Diffuse light from an overcast sky casts no sharp shadows.
The essay's argument is so diffuse that its main point is hard to find.
The smell of popcorn was diffuse, drifting through the whole theater.

confused.note: Diffuse means spread out; to defuse is to remove the fuse from a bomb or calm a tense situation.

questions.passage: The first draft of the speech was ______, wandering across a dozen topics in forty minutes. An editor cut it to three clear points that could be delivered in ten.
questions.explanation: A speech that wanders over many topics is spread out and unfocused.

distractors.why: Unequivocal means clear and direct, the opposite of a wandering draft.
Obtuse means slow to understand, a word for people, not speeches.
Gullible means easily fooled, which does not describe a draft.

partsNote: from Latin fundere, "to pour": poured apart

definition: to make something, especially something bad, continue for a long time

examples.text: The law perpetuated the power of the landowners for another century.
Repeating the flawed method only perpetuates the error.
Forwarding that fake story just perpetuates the rumor.

confused.note: To perpetuate is to make something continue; to perpetrate is to commit a crime.

questions.passage: Textbooks that repeat the story without checking it ______ a myth. Historians showed decades ago that the inventor never said the famous words attributed to him.
questions.explanation: Repeating a false story keeps it alive.

distractors.why: Rectify means to correct, the opposite of spreading a myth.
Perpetrate means to commit a crime; it only resembles the right word.
Surmount means to overcome, which is not what the textbooks do.

partsNote: from Latin petere, "to seek": to carry through

definition: to correct something that is wrong

examples.text: The new treaty rectified the border errors of the old one.
A software update rectified the fault in the sensor.
I rectified my mistake by sending the invitation to the right address.

confused.note: To rectify is to correct; to ratify is to approve formally.

questions.passage: The publisher moved quickly to ______ the error. Within a week it had recalled the misprinted copies, issued a corrected edition, and sent a letter of apology to every bookseller.
questions.explanation: Recalling and reissuing the book corrects the mistake.

distractors.why: Ratify means to approve formally; it resembles the right word but does not mean to correct.
Perpetuate means to make something continue, the opposite of fixing it.
Feign means to pretend, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin rectus, "right, straight": to make right

definition: a trick intended to deceive someone

examples.text: The wooden horse was a ruse to get soldiers inside the city walls.
The detective's sudden illness is a ruse to make the thief careless.
My "I forgot my wallet" ruse no longer works on my friends.

confused.note: A ruse is a trick; to rouse is to wake or stir up.

questions.passage: The telephone call claiming to be from the bank was a ______. Its real purpose was to persuade the elderly customer to read out the numbers on her card.
questions.explanation: A false call meant to steal card numbers is a deceptive trick.

distractors.why: A harbinger is a sign of what is coming, not a trick.
A maverick is an independent person, which does not fit.
Fortitude is courage, which does not describe a deceptive call.

definition: courage and strength in facing pain or difficulty over a long time

examples.text: The settlers bore the first winter with remarkable fortitude.
Her fortitude through years of illness shames the complaining narrator.
It takes fortitude to finish a marathon on a blistered foot.

confused.note: Fortitude is courage in hardship; fortune is luck or wealth.

questions.passage: The polar explorers endured months of darkness, hunger, and cold that froze the ink in their pens. Their diaries, written without complaint, are a record of extraordinary ______.
questions.explanation: Enduring such hardship without complaint shows courage and strength.

distractors.why: Levity means lightheartedness, which is not what the hardships reveal.
Discretion means careful judgment, which is not the quality stressed.
Guile means cunning, which does not fit.

definition: too willing to believe what other people say; easily tricked

examples.text: The gullible farmer trades his cow for a handful of beans.
Gullible investors poured their savings into a mine that did not exist.
I was gullible enough to believe that the word "gullible" is not in the dictionary.

confused.note: Gullible means easily fooled; guileless means honest and without deceit.

questions.passage: The swindler looked for ______ customers. He avoided anyone who asked for references and concentrated on those who nodded along and reached for their wallets before he had finished speaking.
questions.explanation: Customers who believe without question are easily tricked.

distractors.why: Obtuse means slow to understand; the swindler wanted trust, not slowness.
Surly means bad-tempered, which would not make a good target.
Dynamic means energetic, which does not fit.

partsNote: from "gull," an old word for a person who is easily fooled

definition: extremely small

examples.text: The diminutive frog, no longer than a fingernail, lives in leaf litter.
The diminutive general stood on a box to address his troops.
Our diminutive car fits into parking spaces no one else will try.

confused.note: Diminutive means very small in size; diminished means reduced.

questions.passage: Visitors expecting a grand palace are surprised by its ______ size. The famous residence has only six rooms, and its garden could fit inside a tennis court.
questions.explanation: Six rooms and a tiny garden make the palace very small.

distractors.why: Hallowed means sacred, which does not describe size.
Sinister means threatening, which does not fit.
Derivative means unoriginal, which does not describe size.

definition: to feel deep respect and admiration for someone or something

examples.text: The nation revered the old general long after he had left the field.
The students revere their teacher and copy even her handwriting.
My grandmother reveres her cast-iron pan and lets no one else wash it.

confused.note: To revere is to respect deeply; to revert is to go back to an earlier state.

questions.passage: In her village the old midwife was ______. People stood when she entered a room, sought her advice on every important decision, and named their daughters after her.
questions.explanation: Standing, seeking her advice, and naming children for her show deep respect.

distractors.why: Abased means humiliated, the opposite of honored.
Feigned means pretended, which does not fit.
Appraised means judged the value of, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin vereri, "to fear, to respect"

definition: a strong liking for something or a tendency to do it

examples.text: The detective has a penchant for quoting poetry at crime scenes.
The king's penchant for building palaces emptied the treasury.
My dad has a penchant for telling the same joke at every birthday.

confused.note: A penchant is a strong liking; a pendant is a piece of jewelry that hangs from a chain.

questions.passage: The director has a ______ for filming in remote places. Her last three projects were shot on a glacier, in a desert four days' drive from the nearest town, and aboard a fishing boat in winter.
questions.explanation: Repeatedly choosing remote locations shows a strong liking.

distractors.why: An aversion is a strong dislike, the opposite of her repeated choice.
A ruse is a trick, which does not fit.
A harbinger is a forerunner, which does not fit.

definition: slow or unwilling to understand something

examples.text: The obtuse suitor mistakes every polite refusal for encouragement.
Only an obtuse minister could have missed the signs of revolt.
I was being obtuse; she had hinted three times that it was her birthday.

confused.note: Obtuse describes a person who is slow to understand; abstruse describes ideas that are hard to understand.

questions.passage: The guests had yawned, checked their watches, and finally put on their coats. Their host, cheerfully ______, took none of these hints and began another story.
questions.explanation: Missing obvious hints shows slowness to understand.

distractors.why: Perspicacious means keenly perceptive, the opposite of missing every hint.
Surly means bad-tempered, but the host is cheerful.
Callow means young and inexperienced, which is not what the scene shows.

definition: regarded as holy or greatly respected

examples.text: Soldiers of both armies lie in the hallowed ground of the old churchyard.
The poet walks the hallowed halls where her heroes once studied.
To my grandfather, the baseball stadium is hallowed ground.

confused.note: Hallowed means holy or revered; hollowed means emptied out.

questions.passage: To the university's graduates, the old library is ______ ground. Many return decades later simply to sit at the same oak tables where they once studied, and proposals to modernize the building are always fiercely opposed.
questions.explanation: A place alumni treat with such reverence is greatly respected.

distractors.why: Derivative means unoriginal, which does not fit.
Diffuse means spread out, which does not describe a revered place.
Sinister means threatening, the opposite of a beloved place.

definition: completely clear and firm, leaving no doubt

examples.text: The data are unequivocal: the glacier has lost a third of its ice.
The council gave an unequivocal refusal to the king's demand.
Mom's answer to "Can we get a snake?" was an unequivocal no.

confused.note: Unequivocal means leaving no doubt; unequal means not equal.

questions.passage: The committee's verdict was ______. In language that left no room for interpretation, it stated that the bridge was unsafe and must be closed to all traffic that same day.
questions.explanation: A verdict with no room for interpretation is completely clear.

distractors.why: Diffuse means spread out and unfocused, the opposite of this verdict.
Callow means inexperienced, which does not describe a verdict.
Gullible means easily fooled, which does not fit.

definition: to limit or restrict what someone or something can do

examples.text: The size of the telescope's mirror constrains how faint an object it can detect.
The charter constrained the king's power to raise taxes.
A tight budget constrained our choice of vacation to places we could drive.

confused.note: To constrain is to limit; to construe is to interpret.

questions.passage: The architect's design was ______ by the shape of the lot. Because the land was a narrow triangle wedged between two streets, the house could be no more than four meters wide at its front.
questions.explanation: The lot's shape limited what the design could be.

distractors.why: Enhanced means improved, but the lot restricted the design.
Embellished means decorated or exaggerated, which does not fit.
Evaded means escaped or avoided, which does not fit a design and a lot.

definition: to collect a large amount of something over time

examples.text: The merchant amassed a fortune in the spice trade.
Over forty years the observatory amassed records of two million stars.
My little brother has amassed an impressive collection of bottle caps.

confused.note: To amass is to gather in quantity; to amaze is to astonish.

questions.passage: Over half a century the collector quietly ______ more than thirty thousand postcards. When her family opened the attic after her death, they found them sorted by country in two hundred shoeboxes.
questions.explanation: Gathering thirty thousand postcards over decades is collecting a large amount.

distractors.why: Suppressed means held back or put down, which does not fit collecting.
Assessed means evaluated, which does not capture gathering a collection.
Constrained means limited, which does not fit.

partsNote: from "mass": to bring into a mass

definition: intended to end a disagreement or make someone less angry

examples.text: The king's conciliatory letter offered the rebels a full pardon.
She makes a conciliatory gesture, pouring her rival the first cup of tea.
After our argument, my brother left a conciliatory cookie on my desk.

confused.note: Conciliatory aims to make peace; consolatory aims to comfort someone who is sad.

questions.passage: After weeks of angry exchanges, the union's leader adopted a more ______ tone. She praised the company's latest offer as "a serious step" and proposed that both sides meet without lawyers.
questions.explanation: Praise and a proposal to meet show an effort to end the dispute.

distractors.why: Scathing means harshly critical, the opposite of her new tone.
Inscrutable means impossible to read, but her meaning was plain.
Provincial means narrow in outlook, which does not fit.

definition: refusing to change one's mind or behavior; stubborn

examples.text: The obstinate governor rejected every compromise until the city rose against him.
An obstinate mule and an obstinate farmer spend the chapter glaring at each other.
The obstinate stain survived three washes.

confused.note: Obstinate means stubborn; to obstruct is to block.

questions.passage: Doctors, friends, and finally his own children urged the old sailor to stop climbing the mast at eighty. He was ______, insisting that he had done it for sixty years and saw no reason to stop.
questions.explanation: Refusing all advice to stop shows stubbornness.

distractors.why: Conciliatory means willing to make peace, which he was not.
Effusive means gushing with feeling, which does not describe his refusal.
Imminent means about to happen, which does not describe a person.

definition: lightness or humor, especially about a serious matter

examples.text: The senator's levity during the debate on the famine offended his colleagues.
A moment of levity breaks the tension before the duel.
Dad's joke brought some welcome levity to a long day of moving boxes.

confused.note: Levity is lightness or humor; brevity is shortness.

questions.passage: The memorial service was solemn, as expected, but not without ______. The speaker recalled the professor's habit of losing his glasses on top of his own head, and laughter rippled through the hall.
questions.explanation: Laughter at a funny memory brings humor into a serious occasion.

distractors.why: Integrity means honesty, which is not what the laughter added.
Chaos means complete disorder, far too strong for a ripple of laughter.
Brevity means shortness; it sounds similar but does not mean humor.

definition: impossible to understand or interpret

examples.text: The butler's inscrutable face reveals nothing of what he saw.
The emperor's inscrutable silence left the envoys guessing for a week.
My cat gives me an inscrutable stare whenever I ask where my sock went.

confused.note: Inscrutable means impossible to read; unscrupulous means without moral principles.

questions.passage: Opponents found the poker champion ______. Whether she held a winning hand or a worthless one, her expression never changed, and no one could guess what she would do next.
questions.explanation: A face that never changes cannot be read.

distractors.why: Effusive means openly gushing, the opposite of revealing nothing.
Notorious means famous for something bad, which is not the point.
Squalid means dirty and wretched, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin scrutari, "to search": not able to be searched out

definition: to make something more attractive by adding details; or to add untrue details to a story

examples.text: Monks embellished the first letter of each chapter with gold leaf.
The old sailor embellishes his tale a little more with every telling.
I may have embellished the size of the fish I caught.

confused.note: To embellish is to decorate or exaggerate; to embezzle is to steal entrusted money.

questions.passage: The explorer's first report of the journey was plain and accurate. In later lectures he began to ______ it, adding a storm that had never occurred and a tiger that grew larger with each telling.
questions.explanation: Adding invented details makes the story more impressive but less true.

distractors.why: Suppress means to hold back, but he was adding material.
Assess means to evaluate, which is not what he did to his story.
Constrain means to limit, the opposite of adding to the story.

definition: expressing feelings, especially praise or thanks, in an unrestrained way

examples.text: The aunt's effusive greeting involves three kisses and a shriek.
The mayor offered effusive thanks to the engineers who had saved the harbor.
My grandmother is effusive about every drawing I have ever made.

confused.note: Effusive means gushing; elusive means hard to catch.

questions.passage: The critic, usually sparing with compliments, was ______ in her praise of the young pianist. Her review used the word "astonishing" four times and ended by calling the concert the finest she had heard in a decade.
questions.explanation: Repeated superlatives are unrestrained praise.

distractors.why: Scathing means harshly critical, the opposite of this review.
Moderate means restrained, but her praise was unrestrained.
Acute means sharp or severe, which does not describe generous praise.

partsNote: from Latin fundere, "to pour": pouring out

definition: cruel and unfair in the use of power; or uncomfortably heavy, hot, or severe

examples.text: The oppressive regime jailed anyone who criticized the president.
The oppressive humidity of the rainforest fogged every lens.
The oppressive heat in the gym made practice miserable.

confused.note: Oppressive means cruelly controlling or heavy; aggressive means ready to attack.

questions.passage: Under the new laws, farmers had to hand over half of every harvest and could not leave their villages without a permit. Many found the rules so ______ that they abandoned their land and fled across the border.
questions.explanation: Rules harsh enough to drive farmers from their land are cruel and unfair.

distractors.why: Conciliatory means aimed at making peace, which these rules were not.
Moderate means mild and reasonable, the opposite of these demands.
Inscrutable means impossible to understand; the rules were clear and harsh.

partsNote: from Latin premere, "to press": pressing against

definition: to escape or avoid something, especially by being clever or dishonest

examples.text: The smugglers evaded customs officers by landing at night.
Some viruses evade the immune system by changing their outer coats.
My brother evaded dish duty by claiming he had homework.

confused.note: To evade is to escape or avoid; to invade is to enter by force.

questions.passage: The senator did not refuse to answer the reporter's question. She simply ______ it, speaking at length about her record on unrelated issues until the time allotted for the interview had run out.
questions.explanation: Talking about other things until time ran out avoids the question.

distractors.why: Assessed means evaluated, which is not what she did with the question.
Amassed means gathered in quantity, which does not fit.
Embellished means added details to, but she avoided the question entirely.

partsNote: from Latin vadere, "to go": to go out from

definition: severely and harshly critical

examples.text: The scathing review ended the play's run after three nights.
The inquiry's scathing report blamed the admiral for the loss of the fleet.
My sister gave my outfit a scathing look and said nothing, which was worse.

confused.note: Scathing means harshly critical; seething means boiling with anger.

questions.passage: The auditors' report was ______. It described the agency's accounts as "a work of fiction," its managers as "asleep at their desks," and its past statements to the public as "simply untrue."
questions.explanation: Calling accounts fiction and managers asleep is harsh criticism.

distractors.why: Effusive means gushing with praise, the opposite of this report.
Conciliatory means peacemaking, which these insults were not.
Provincial means narrow in outlook, which does not describe the report.

definition: a sign that something, especially something important, is going to happen

examples.text: The first robin is a harbinger of spring.
The riots in the port were a harbinger of the revolution to come.
The smell of cinnamon is a harbinger of the holidays at our house.

confused.note: A harbinger is a sign of what is coming; a harbor is a sheltered port.

questions.passage: Economists watch the price of copper closely. Because the metal is used in nearly everything that is built, a sudden drop in demand for it is often a ______ of wider trouble.
questions.explanation: A drop in copper demand signals that trouble is coming.

distractors.why: Levity is lightheartedness, which does not fit.
Integrity is honesty, which does not fit "of wider trouble."
An incumbent is a current officeholder, which does not fit.

definition: very dirty and unpleasant, especially because of poverty or neglect

examples.text: Reformers photographed the squalid tenements to shame the city into action.
The orphan's squalid room has a broken window and a single blanket.
After a week of camping in the rain, our tent was squalid.

confused.note: Squalid means filthy; a squall is a sudden violent wind.

questions.passage: Inspectors were shocked by the ______ conditions in the workers' quarters. Twelve men shared a single unheated room, water came from a rusted barrel, and rats ran along the rafters.
questions.explanation: Crowding, rusty water, and rats describe filthy, wretched conditions.

distractors.why: Oppressive means harsh or stifling; the details stress filth and neglect.
Moderate means reasonable, which these conditions were not.
Acute means sharp or severe, which does not capture dirt and neglect.

definition: to spread and divide into branches; to have complicated results

examples.text: The nerve ramifies into thousands of tiny fibers.
The scandal ramified through every department of the government.
One small lie ramified into a whole week of excuses.

confused.note: To ramify is to branch out; to ratify is to approve formally.

questions.passage: The effects of the new tax did not stay confined to the shipping industry. They ______ in unexpected directions, raising the price of bread in inland towns and closing workshops that had never sent a single crate by sea.
questions.explanation: Effects spreading in many directions branch out.

distractors.why: Suppressed means held back, which does not fit spreading effects.
Converged means came together at a point, the opposite of spreading outward.
Evaded means escaped, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin ramus, "branch": to make branches

definition: complete disorder and confusion

examples.text: After the king fled, the capital fell into chaos.
The equations show how tiny changes can turn order into chaos.
The kitchen was chaos by the time we finished making the birthday cake.

confused.note: Chaos is total disorder; a chasm is a deep opening in the ground.

questions.passage: When the power failed during rush hour, the station descended into ______. Signs went dark, announcements stopped, and thousands of passengers pushed in opposite directions along unlit platforms.
questions.explanation: Dark signs and crowds pushing in every direction are total disorder.

distractors.why: Levity is lightheartedness, which this scene lacks.
Integrity is honesty or soundness, which does not fit.
Discretion is careful judgment, which does not describe the scene.

definition: not extreme; average in amount, size, or degree

examples.text: The plant grows best in moderate temperatures.
Moderate members of the council tried to calm both factions.
A moderate amount of salt improves the soup; a handful ruins it.

confused.note: Moderate means not extreme; modest means humble or fairly small.

questions.passage: The storm was neither a gentle shower nor the hurricane that forecasters had feared. It brought ______ winds and steady rain, enough to cancel the parade but not to damage a single roof.
questions.explanation: Winds between gentle and severe are not extreme.

distractors.why: Oppressive means harshly heavy, too strong for a storm that damaged nothing.
Imminent means about to happen, which does not describe wind strength.
Scathing means harshly critical, a word for criticism, not weather.

definition: the quality of being honest and having strong moral principles; or wholeness

examples.text: Even his enemies never questioned the judge's integrity.
The crack threatened the structural integrity of the dam.
Returning the extra change showed real integrity.

confused.note: Integrity is honesty or wholeness; integration is the combining of parts.

questions.passage: The accountant was offered a large bonus to overlook the missing funds. Her ______ would not allow it: she reported the matter the same day, though she knew it might cost her the job.
questions.explanation: Refusing a bribe and reporting wrongdoing shows honesty and principle.

distractors.why: Levity is lightheartedness, which is not what made her act.
Chaos is disorder, which does not fit.
Discretion means tact or keeping quiet, the opposite of reporting the matter.

definition: narrow in outlook; or relating to regions outside the capital

examples.text: Provincial governors answered to the emperor only once a year.
The heroine finds her hometown stifling and provincial after a year abroad.
It is provincial to assume that every country eats dinner at six.

confused.note: Provincial means narrow or regional; providential means lucky, as if by divine care.

questions.passage: Having never traveled more than fifty miles from his birthplace, the young critic had a decidedly ______ outlook. He judged every foreign novel by how closely it resembled the books written in his own town.
questions.explanation: Judging everything by local standards shows a narrow outlook.

distractors.why: Cosmopolitan means worldly, the opposite of his outlook.
Conciliatory means peacemaking, which does not fit.
Effusive means gushing, which is not the trait described.

definition: to judge the nature, quality, or value of something

examples.text: Divers assessed the damage to the reef after the oil spill.
A commission was sent to assess the colony's defenses.
The coach assessed each player's sprint time on the first day.

confused.note: To assess is to evaluate; access is the ability to enter or use.

questions.passage: Before prescribing any treatment, the physiotherapist must ______ the injury. She watches the patient walk, tests the strength of each muscle, and measures how far the joint can bend.
questions.explanation: Watching, testing, and measuring evaluate the injury.

distractors.why: Enhance means to improve, which she would not do to an injury.
Evade means to avoid, which is not her task.
Embellish means to decorate or exaggerate, which does not fit.

partsNote: to sit beside as a judge

definition: to improve the quality, value, or attractiveness of something

examples.text: Adding iron to the soil enhanced the plants' growth.
The victory enhanced the young general's reputation.
A squeeze of lime enhances the flavor of almost any taco.

confused.note: To enhance is to improve in quality; to augment is to increase in size or amount.

questions.passage: The museum installed softer lighting and repainted its walls a deep gray. Both changes were intended to ______ visitors' experience of the paintings, whose colors now appear far richer.
questions.explanation: Changes that make colors appear richer improve the experience.

distractors.why: Constrain means to limit, the opposite of improving.
Suppress means to hold down, which was not the intention.
Assess means to evaluate; the changes were meant to improve, not to judge.

definition: very serious or severe; or very sharp and perceptive

examples.text: The patient was admitted with acute pain in the lower back.
The shortage of grain became acute in the third year of the drought.
Dogs have an acute sense of smell, as mine proves at every picnic.

confused.note: Acute problems are sudden and severe; chronic problems last a long time.

questions.passage: The city has always been short of housing, but in the past two years the shortage has become ______. Rents have doubled, and families who once waited months for an apartment now wait years.
questions.explanation: Doubled rents and years-long waits show the shortage has become severe.

distractors.why: Moderate means not extreme, the opposite of a worsening crisis.
Provincial means narrow in outlook, which does not describe a shortage.
Squalid means filthy, which does not describe a shortage.

definition: famous for something bad

examples.text: The notorious pirate was finally captured off the coast in 1720.
The village's notorious gossip knows every secret before it happens.
Our street is notorious for potholes that swallow bicycle wheels.

confused.note: Notorious means famous for something bad; notable means worthy of notice, usually for something good.

questions.passage: The intersection is ______ among local drivers. More accidents occur there than anywhere else in the county, and insurance companies charge higher rates to those who live nearby.
questions.explanation: A place known for accidents is famous for something bad.

distractors.why: Hallowed means revered, the opposite of a dreaded intersection.
Inscrutable means impossible to understand, which is not the point.
Conciliatory means peacemaking, which does not fit.

definition: currently holding an official position; or necessary as a duty

examples.text: The incumbent governor lost to a challenger half her age.
It is incumbent on researchers to report results that contradict their own theories.
It is incumbent on the last person out to lock the door.

confused.note: Incumbent means currently in office or required; recumbent means lying down.

questions.passage: Challengers in the election face a familiar difficulty. The ______ mayor has held office for twelve years, is known to every voter, and can point to roads and schools built during her terms.
questions.explanation: A mayor now in office is the incumbent.

distractors.why: Imminent means about to happen, which does not describe a mayor in office.
Notorious means famous for something bad, but her record is presented favorably.
Obstinate means stubborn, which is not the point.

partsNote: from Latin cumbere, "to lie": resting upon

definition: about to happen very soon

examples.text: Rising pressure inside the volcano suggested that an eruption was imminent.
With the enemy at the gates, the city's fall seemed imminent.
The dark clouds made it clear that rain was imminent.

confused.note: Imminent means about to happen; eminent means distinguished.

questions.passage: Sensors beneath the glacier recorded hundreds of small tremors in a single day. Scientists warned that a collapse was ______ and ordered the valley below to be evacuated at once.
questions.explanation: Tremors and an immediate evacuation show the collapse is about to happen.

distractors.why: Eminent means distinguished; it only looks like the right word.
Incumbent means currently in office or required as a duty, which does not fit.
Acute means severe; the warning is about timing, that the collapse is near.

partsNote: from Latin minere, "to project, to overhang"

definition: to stop something by force; or to prevent something from being seen, expressed, or known

examples.text: The army was sent to suppress the uprising.
The drug suppresses the body's immune response.
I suppressed a laugh when my teacher's wig slipped.

confused.note: To suppress is to put down or hold back something; to oppress is to treat people cruelly.

questions.passage: The company did not publish the unfavorable results. Instead it tried to ______ them, instructing its researchers not to discuss the study and omitting it from the annual report.
questions.explanation: Silencing researchers and omitting the study keeps the results from being known.

distractors.why: Enhance means to improve, which is not what the company did to the results.
Embellish means to add flattering details; the company hid the results entirely.
Amass means to gather, which does not fit.

partsNote: from Latin premere, "to press": to press under
